name: libvirt
license: LGPL 2.1 or later (library); some tools GPL 2.0 or later
summary: A stable API, daemon and `virsh` command line for managing virtual machines, storage and networks, with drivers for QEMU/KVM, Xen, LXC, Cloud Hypervisor, VMware ESX, Hyper-V and more.
intro: libvirt sits between management tools and hypervisors. A program, or the `virsh` shell, opens a connection with a URI that names a driver and an instance: `qemu:///system` reaches the root-owned daemon that runs server VMs with access to host devices and networks, `qemu:///session` a per-user daemon whose VMs have only that user’s privileges, `qemu+ssh://host/system` the same on another machine, and `test:///default` an in-memory fake driver for trying the API. The documented hypervisor drivers are QEMU/KVM/HVF, Xen, LXC, Cloud Hypervisor, bhyve, VirtualBox, VMware ESX and Workstation/Player, Microsoft Hyper-V, OpenVZ and Virtuozzo. Most run inside a libvirt daemon on the host; the ESX and Hyper-V drivers instead run in the client and talk to the vSphere SOAP API or to WS-Management over HTTPS.

A VM is a domain, described in XML: `<domain type='kvm'>` (or `qemu`, `xen`, `hvf`), its vCPUs, memory, disks, network interfaces and consoles. `virsh define` stores the definition and `virsh start` runs it. For QEMU, libvirt turns the XML into a QEMU command line, starts the process, and then controls it over QMP, QEMU’s JSON protocol. Around domains, libvirt manages storage pools (directories, LVM, NFS, iSCSI, Ceph RBD, ZFS and more), split into volumes that become guest disks, and virtual networks in NAT, routed, open or isolated modes with DHCP and DNS. The original single daemon, `libvirtd`, is being replaced by one daemon per driver: `virtqemud`, `virtxend`, `virtlxcd`, `virtnetworkd`, `virtstoraged` and others.

The C library is LGPL 2.1 or later, with official bindings for Python, Go, Perl, Java, OCaml, PHP, Ruby and C#. Releases come out on the 1st of each month (11 a year), and the version number tracks time, not features: 12.0.0 came out in January 2026 and the latest is 12.8.0 (October 1, 2026). It is the layer under virt-manager, OpenStack Nova’s default libvirt driver and KubeVirt, where every VM pod runs its own libvirt daemon.
strengths: One API and one XML format for many hypervisors, with an API and ABI the project guarantees to keep stable forever
More than VMs: storage pools, virtual networks, firewall filters, host device and secret management, snapshots and live migration through the same API
Remote management built in, over SSH or TLS, plus a read-only socket for monitoring tools
The common foundation of the Linux virtualization stack: virt-manager, OpenStack Nova and KubeVirt all use it, and bindings exist for most languages
limits: Drivers are uneven: the ESX driver’s documentation still names ESX 3.5 to 5.x, and the Hyper-V driver is client-side only and can’t use libvirt’s remote transport
Manages one host at a time: there is no scheduler or cluster view, so fleets need a platform such as OpenStack or KubeVirt on top
A read-write connection to a system-mode daemon is equivalent to a root shell, so access must be locked down
Two deployment styles coexist while the monolithic `libvirtd` gives way to modular daemons, which changes the services and config files a host needs

sections.title: Hypervisor drivers and their connection URIs
sections.intro: A few of the drivers listed in libvirt’s documentation, with the URI a client uses to reach each one.

items.name: QEMU/KVM
items.text: Runs QEMU processes, with KVM acceleration on Linux or HVF on macOS, in system or session mode, served by `virtqemud`.

items.name: Xen
items.text: Manages VMs on the Xen hypervisor, in system mode only, through `virtxend`.

items.name: LXC
items.text: Runs Linux containers, isolated with namespaces and limited with cgroups, through the same API, served by `virtlxcd`.

items.name: Cloud Hypervisor
items.text: Manages VMs on the Cloud Hypervisor VMM; recent releases added disk and NIC hotplug and SEV-SNP guests.

items.name: VMware ESX
items.text: Client-side: talks to ESX(i) or vCenter over the SOAP-based vSphere API, with nothing installed on the server.

items.name: Microsoft Hyper-V
items.text: Client-side: talks to Hyper-V 2012 R2 and newer over WS-Management (HTTPS or HTTP).

story: In 2005 Xen had brought virtualization to open-source systems, managed through its own daemon, `xend`. On November 2, 2005, Daniel Veillard at Red Hat made the first commit of a small C library to give programs a stable API to Xen. It was called `libxen`, then `libvir`, and in February 2006 it was renamed libvirt. Version 0.0.1 came out on December 19, 2005.

That goal became real in February 2007, when Daniel P. Berrangé added QEMU support, released in 0.2.0, just as KVM was arriving in Linux. Drivers for LXC, VirtualBox, VMware ESX, Hyper-V, bhyve and Cloud Hypervisor followed, along with storage pools, virtual networks and remote access, so desktop tools like virt-manager and cloud platforms like OpenStack could manage VMs without knowing each hypervisor’s details.

libvirt 1.0.0 shipped in November 2012. From 2.0.0 in July 2016 version numbers became time-based, with the major version going up at each January release; it reached 12.0.0 in January 2026, and it now ships 11 releases a year.

choices.choice: A stable API in front of every hypervisor
choices.why: Management tools outlive hypervisor versions. libvirt promises its API and ABI stay stable forever, and each driver maps the same calls and XML onto its own hypervisor.
A domain, network or storage pool is one declarative document that can be stored, edited, diffed and passed to `define`, rather than a long series of API calls or a hypervisor-specific command line.

choices.choice: A privileged daemon, reached by URI
choices.why: Starting VMs, creating bridges and opening disks need root, so that work happens in a daemon and clients connect by URI, locally or over SSH or TLS. Session mode adds a per-user daemon whose VMs get no extra privileges, and the newer modular daemons give each driver its own process.
The C API is LGPL 2.1 or later, so management applications under any license can link to it.
